extracted.intended_audience: business executives, advertising managers, public-relations counselors, and political campaign managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing large-scale propaganda, advertising and public-relations campaigns for business and political purposes, including strategy, budgeting, media coordination, audience analysis, crisis handling, and use of staged events and endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize inter-commodity and inter-industrial competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that new competition operates between products used alternatively for the same purpose (inter-commodity) and between apparently unrelated industries which affect each other or compete for consumer dollars (inter-industrial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan campaigns on the basis that many industries now compete indirectly for the same consumer attention and dollars; trade associations must cooperate because these competitions 'cannot be fought single-handed.' Examples: food producers (fruit vs. potatoes), producers vying for substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda as a complement to advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition will be not only advertising between products or associations but also a 'competition of propaganda' — employing mass dramatization, events, endorsements and mass media to shape public opinion about a product or issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large nationwide radio hook-ups and star performers (e.g., Dodge Victory Six launch) can concentrate attention; treat such events as 'sugar-coated sales messages' that create mass awareness beyond simple ad placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh celebrity endorsements and large spectacles by cost-benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that hiring celebrities increases the cost of advertising and may add little intrinsic product value, so assess whether the extra expense yields required return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern sales technicians aim to 'reduce cost' and improve advertising efficiency; calculate whether celebrity fees increase sales sufficiently to justify expense (example: Galli-Curci singing for bacon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate standardized products by non-price appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: When mass production reduces cost and commoditizes products, develop sales appeals other than cheapness to create perceived originality or style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minor product modifications (color, styling) and social-style campaigns to establish minor elements as matters of fashion; this can split mass markets and protect margins (typewriter colors example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply social-psychology principles to persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use propagandist principles such as gregariousness, obedience to authority, and emulation to popularize minor elements into matters of style or preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly use authoritative figures, trendsetters, and visible exemplars to make an attribute socially desirable (fashion committees, artists, mannequins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize credible committees and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring together respected individuals — society leaders, style experts, fashion editors, artists — to lend authority and legitimacy to the promoted idea or style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form style committees, artist panels, and downtown events to create newsworthy moments that will be transmitted through press and advertising (millinery fashion fete example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use staged public events to dramatize and popularize change
rubrics_metrics.description: Create spectacles (shows, tableaux, inaugurations, exhibitions) that present the idea before trade and consumers to alter buying habits and generate news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate parades, fashion fêtes, exhibitions, contests, or institutes to dramatize the product/issue; the millinery show led to thousands of large hat sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle rumors and crises promptly and technically
rubrics_metrics.description: When false rumors threaten reputation or stock value, act quickly and with proper technical public-relations handling to avert loss of prestige and money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counteract false reports with authoritative local testimonials and community events (Beech-Nut hometown testimonial) and rapid correction through official channels (ticker corrections example for Hudson stock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your public continuously (continuous audience study)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a continuous finger on the public pulse; understand changes in public mind and be prepared to interpret and modify messaging accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensive study of public tastes and scientific market analysis should inform product manufacture and messaging; adapt as public knowledge and taste evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define campaign objectives first and express them clearly (platform)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to determine objectives and express them exceedingly well in current form (e.g., a clear platform) before planning propaganda operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the platform or product promise is honest and credible; campaign pledges should carry a guarantee-like quality to restore public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct scientific analysis and market segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform as nearly scientific an analysis as possible of the public and its needs; identify interlocking groups (economic, social, religious, local, etc.) and target appeals accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys and market study to decide where to focus effort and to inform both messaging and possible product changes; avoid wasting resources 'reselling' already committed segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget campaign expenditures with business-like precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how much money must be raised and budget campaign expenditures carefully, allocating funds to advertising, promotion, supervising personnel, and special events proportionately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use business precedent to calculate campaign costs and allocate percentages to newspaper/magazine ads, outdoors, circularization, dealer aids, and supervising field staff; coordinate spending with overall strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise funds candidly and publicly where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Money-raising campaigns conducted candidly and publicly (modeled after charity drives) would increase political prestige and public participation and reduce corrupt 'black bag' perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent fundraising improves public confidence and can be planned as part of the overall campaign schedule and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate media tasks according to their strengths and coordinate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what each medium (radio, press, speeches, pictures, motion pictures, banners, etc.) can do best, and synchronize them with the whole plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate printed word, pictures, sound, and staged events so one method supports the others; avoid isolated, uncoordinated emotional stunts that waste effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use emotions strategically and in alignment with campaign plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional appeals are indispensable but must (a) coincide with the broad plan, (b) be adapted to target groups, and (c) conform to the media used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional symbolism (e.g., kissing babies) must epitomize a specific plank or policy and be synchronized, not haphazard. Unrelated emotions become maudlin and costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize issues to precondition audience attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Create circumstances that make the contention dramatic and self-evident before addressing the public directly; preconditioning increases receptivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: stage low-tariff exhibitions in many cities, have prominent people inaugurate events, organize boycotts or social demonstrations to dramatize the issue prior to radio speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time announcements and events for maximum media impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose timing (day/date) and media windows to maximize press space and public attention (e.g., schedule for Monday rather than Sunday so press has space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masaryk example: change announcement date so cables/press give more coverage; think in terms of global news cycles when scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and recruit professional propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Political organizations (and businesses) should cultivate men trained in publicity and propaganda techniques, possibly apprenticing them in theater or professional publicity before deploying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sending recruits to work with professional publicists or theatrical producers to learn presentation and staging prior to political employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate reach, frequency and cost-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure and estimate how many times target populations will be exposed to messages and calculate cost per converted vote or buyer to judge efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like business subdivisions of circulation and calculation of exposures, political campaigns should compute cost-per-possible-changed-vote (Emily Newell Blair example: $15.27 per possible vote on a speaking tour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on personality; emphasize program and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: While personality helps, the party's program and the candidate's ability to carry it out should be emphasized over mere charm or charisma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personality can transmute interest but should not replace clear demonstration that the candidate can implement the platform; Henry Ford is known for product, not merely personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate local and national efforts to minimize wasteful duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how national campaigns duplicate local campaigns and plan to reduce unnecessary repetition and expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When budgeting, calculate overlap and avoid redundant placements that add little marginal effect but increase cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use endorsements and community recognition to neutralize damaging claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy community testimonials, civic recognition, and prominent local ceremonies to discredit rumors or hostile assertions more convincingly than a mere denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beech-Nut hometown celebration is an example where community endorsement created stronger conviction than a simple denial would have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create varied and innovative channels for dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond radio and press, invent exhibitions, contests, educational cooperation, and dramatic group cooperations to present ideas to previously untapped publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think expansively about venues and events that can dramatize issues to different groupings; do not limit to traditional stump and radio formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure messaging conforms to the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the message form to the medium: oratory, pictures, motion pictures, radio, posters each have different capacities and constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A campaign should decide which emotions and symbols can be effectively conveyed by each medium and synchronize content accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain honesty and social responsibility in propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda that is untrue or unsocial will weaken as the public becomes more sophisticated; truthful and socially responsible messaging endures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepts that propaganda is an instrument but warns against dishonest use; the public's increased intelligence will punish untruths while fair propaganda remains effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage group leaders and interlocking group structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and establish contact with group leaders who influence the opinions of their constituencies, and coordinate appeals across interlocking social groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aligning actors (and their audiences) with a candidate, building coalitions (mothers, educators, physicians) for legislative success (Shepard-Towner example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use product/issue analysis to inform both product design and messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Market analysis often leads to basic product changes as well as decisions on presentation; advertising strategy should be informed by product improvement opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business practice: analyze markets before making or selling; let analysis prompt product improvements as well as targeted presentation and media choice.
